You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Diagnosis:
The failing test case tests the inverseCumulativeProbability method of the FDistribution class with very large degrees of freedom (200000, 200000) and checks that the inverse cumulative probability for 0.01 is less than 1.0. According to the comment in the test, the failure was due to inaccurate results from ContinuedFraction, indicating numerical or accuracy problems in approximations used in the calculation. The current bug report describes a similar class of problem but for the BinomialDistribution - incorrect inverse cumulative probability results for large parameters due to inaccuracies in the cumulativeProbability method. Thus, the issue likely is general inaccuracies or inefficiencies in the inverse cumulative probability calculation for large input parameters in the related distributions.

The FDistribution constructors show no special handling for large degrees of freedom beyond parameter checking and setting accuracy. The cumulativeProbability method calls Beta.regularizedBeta with an expression based on the degrees of freedom and input x, which is crucial for computation of the cumulative distribution function. The inverseCumulativeProbability method (not directly retrieved but likely implemented by a solve root-finding on cumulativeProbability - this is a common pattern) depends on this cumulativeProbability being accurate and numerically stable, and on the solving method's accuracy and robustness.

Given the test comment, the failure likely occurs due to accumulated numerical inaccuracies of the ContinuedFraction approximation inside the Beta regularized function or the root-finder used in inverseCumulativeProbability for large input parameters. The Beta regularized function may become unstable or inaccurate for very large degrees of freedom, leading to errors in both cumulativeProbability and inverseCumulativeProbability.

The current bug report supports this hypothesis: it argues that for BinomialDistribution, inverseCumulativeProbability gives wrong results for large parameters due to the cumulativeProbability method inaccuracies. This analogy strengthens the suspicion that the implementation of cumulativeProbability and numerical methods used in inverseCumulativeProbability for large parameters need improvement or special handling to maintain accuracy and stability.

Recent bug reports were unrelated and thus not helpful for the diagnosis.

Next, checking the implementation of inverseCumulativeProbability and the numerical solvers it uses would be needed to see how the root finding is performed and whether there are ways to improve the approach to handle large parameters accurately.

Summary: The bug is caused by numerical inaccuracies in the cumulativeProbability computation (via the Beta regularized function) and/or the numerical solver in inverseCumulativeProbability under large degrees of freedom or large parameters, leading to incorrect inverse cumulative probability results as shown in the test. The similar current report on BinomialDistribution supports this being a general problem for large distribution parameters.

I will now investigate the inverseCumulativeProbability method and the numerical solver used to locate more concrete causes.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
